Meteg after the primary stress

Alternately, you can click on an individual Hebrew word to toggle only that word's spacing.

A meteg almost always comes before the stressed syllable of its word, but it can also come after the stress. MAM has 232 cases of meteg after the stress (MAS). For example:

Gen. 22:7 הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י

In this document, by "word" we mean either a simple word (having just one atom) or a compound word (having two or more atoms connected by maqaf marks). By "atom", we mean a sequence of pointed letters uninterrupted by space, maqaf, or any other punctuation.

MAS census by cantillation system

cant-sys words MBS MAS % MAS
prose 233,586 13,091 178 1.3%
poetic 29,605 1,814 54 2.9%
all 263,191 14,905 232 1.5%

So a meteg comes before the stress 14,905 times and after it 232 times. See the Methods.

Facts about MAS

  • In every MAS case, the stress syllable has a conjunctive accent (φ1).
  • In every MAS case, the MAS syllable comes right after the stress syllable.
  • In every MAS case except four (φ2), the MAS syllable is final.
  • In every MAS case but one (φ3), the next word has initial stress.
  • In 93.5% of MAS cases (φ4), the next word has a disjunctive accent.

The three types of MAS

All but 7 cases of MAS can be sorted into one of the three following types: (φ5)

  1. The MAS is on an open final syllable.
  2. The word is closed by a guttural.
  3. The MAS is on a closed, final, tsere-vowelled syllable. (φ6)
Type Prose Poetic All Example
1 113 10 123 הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י
2 34 26 60 תַּצְמִ֣יחַֽ לָ֑ךְ
3 26 16 42 וַיָּ֣צֵֽץ צִ֔יץ
misc 5 2 7 וַיֹּ֥אמֶֽר ׀ לֹ֖א

The 232 individual cases are listed separately and can be filtered by type. The 7 misc cases appear in that large list, but are also further discussed on a page of their own.

The four subtypes of MAS type 1

All cases of MAS type 1 can be sorted into one of the four following subtypes:

  • 1A: The next word has initial stress and an initial vocal shewa. (φ7)
  • 1B: The next word has a pashta stress helper on its first letter. (φ8)
  • 1C: Like 1B, but with some accent other than pashta.
  • 1D: The next word does not have initial stress.
Subtype Prose Poetic All Example
1A 97 6 103 הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י
1B 12 0 12 וְעָ֤שָֽׂה פֶ֙סַח֙
1C 3 4 7 יַעְלִ֩ימֽוּ֩ עַ֨ם
1D 1 0 1 וְהַשְׁמִ֣יעֽוּ בְמִגְדּ֔וֹל

The three subtypes of MAS type 2

All cases of MAS type 2 can be sorted into one of the three following subtypes:

  • 2A: The next word begins with ל (lamed).
  • 2B: The next word begins with a guttural.
  • 2C: The next word begins with neither ל nor a guttural.
Subtype Prose Poetic All Example
2A 26 12 38 תַּצְמִ֣יחַֽ לָ֑ךְ
2B 7 10 17 רֹצֵ֣חַֽ ה֑וּא
2C 1 4 5 בּ֤וֹקֵֽעַ מַ֙יִם֙

Fit for MAS

It is natural to ask how often a MAS actually appears in situations fit for a MAS. The answer is that a MAS appears 52.5% of the time in situations fit for MAS, but the “yield” varies widely between types 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B, and 3. Notably, the type 3 “yield” is 100%.

"Fit for MAS" is analogous to the broader idea of a syllable fit for a meteg. A potential MAS syllable is fit for MAS when:

  • The potential MAS syllable comes immediately after a nonfinal stress syllable with a conjunctive accent.
  • The next word has initial stress and a disjunctive accent.
  • The word does not already have a meteg.
  • The potential MAS syllable is type 1A, type 1B, type 2A, type 2B, or type 3.

The Fit for MAS table records how often MAS occurs in situations that meet these criteria and how often MAS does not occur.

Type Fit for MAS Has MAS % has MAS Lacks MAS
1A 196 89 45.4% 107
1B 41 12 29.3% 29
2A 40 35 87.5% 5
2B 45 14 31.1% 31
3 40 40 100.0% 0
any 362 190 52.5% 172

The 172 cases fit for MAS that lack MAS are listed separately and can be filtered by subtype.

The final-row "Has MAS" count is 190, rather than the total of 232 MAS cases, because 42 syllables have MAS even though the Fit for MAS definition does not consider the syllables fit for MAS. The table shows why the surprising MAS cases are not fit for MAS.

Footnotes

φ1 — A meteg after silluq in Leningrad

In the Leningrad Codex, the last word of 1 Samuel 17:5 seems to have a meteg after its silluq.

Although that meteg is pretty surprising, we deem it less surprising than if we interpret the marks in meteg-silluq order. In silluq-meteg order, only the presence of the meteg is surprising; in meteg-silluq order, the location of the stress is surprising. We find a meteg surprise far more likely than a stress surprise.

This surprising meteg is correctly recorded in BHS and in BHS-derived editions such as UXLC and WLC:

MAM נְחֹֽשֶׁת׃
BHS נְחֹֽשֶֽׁת׃

A meteg after a silluq is hard to identify in Unicode, since the two marks share one codepoint.

φ2 — The four nonfinal MAS syllables

The four exceptions are all MAS cases of subtype 2C: each MAS syllable is an open penultimate tsere syllable before a final furtive-pataḥ syllable.

Isa. 63:12 בּ֤וֹקֵֽעַ מַ֙יִם֙
Prov. 1:19 כׇּל־בֹּ֣צֵֽעַ בָּ֑צַע
Prov. 11:26 מֹ֣נֵֽעַ בָּ֭ר
Job 5:10 וְשֹׁ֥לֵֽחַ מַ֝֗יִם

φ3 — Next word lacking initial stress

At Jer. 46:14, the word after the MAS lacks initial stress: וְהַשְׁמִ֣יעֽוּ בְמִגְדּ֔וֹל.

φ5 — Sources for types 1–3

The three types of MAS are described in both ITM and CoS. Exactly what words are included and excluded in these three types vary between ITM, CoS, and our document here, but they broadly agree.

φ6 — Do types 2 and 3 overlap?

Types 2 and 3 could in principle overlap. However, 56 of the 60 type-2 MAS syllables have pataḥ, and while the other 4 have tsere, that syllable is not only open but also nonfinal. Thus no type-2 MAS meets the type-3 condition. Indeed, words with a final tsere syllable closed by a guttural are quite rare even without a meteg. Only 154 words have a final tsere syllable closed by a guttural. All 154 occur in Aramaic and end in a mappiq he: 136 are in Daniel and 18 are in Ezra. For example:

Dan. 2:5 וּפִשְׁרֵ֔הּ

φ7 — Vocal shewa and initial stress

We don't consider vocal shewa to be a syllable, so a word with an initial vocal shewa can still have initial stress.

φ8 — A pashta stress helper on the first letter

Because this word has a pashta stress helper on its first letter, we know that it does not have an initial vocal shewa.
